2027-07-31.title: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Priest
readings: In this year of jubilee you shall return, every one of you, to your property
O God, let all the nations praise you!
Herod sent and had John beheaded in the prison
2027-07-31.alt: Memorial. The weekday readings of Week 17 (Year I) are given; the proper readings of the memorial (1 Corinthians 10:31–11:1; Luke 14:25–33) may be used instead. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-31.verse: And you shall hallow the fiftieth year and you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you: you shall return, every one of you, to your property and every one of you to your family.
theo: The first reading gives the law of the Jubilee, spoken “on Mount Sinai.” Israel is to count seven weeks of years, “seven times seven years,” forty-nine years, and then, “on the tenth day of the seventh month, on the day of atonement,” the trumpet is to be sounded “throughout all your land.” The fiftieth year is holy: “you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you: you shall return, every one of you, to your property and every one of you to your family.” The land is not to be sown or reaped that year; it rests, and the people eat what the field gives by itself. Property that has been sold or lost returns to the family; those who have fallen into debt are released. In effect the Jubilee is a reset, a time when the poor are given back what they have lost and no family is shut out of the land for ever. There are practical rules as well: in buying and selling, “you shall not cheat one another,” and the price is to reflect the number of harvests before the next Jubilee, “but you shall fear your God; for I am the Lord your God.” The year of Jubilee became, for the prophets, a picture of God's saving freedom. Jesus read from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth: “to proclaim release to the captives... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (Luke 4:18–19). The Church keeps Holy Years of Jubilee, the most recent in 2025. The Psalm is a prayer for the blessing to reach beyond Israel: “May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, that your way may be known upon earth, your saving power among all nations.”

The Gospel shows the opposite of liberty: a prophet in prison and a king in bondage to his own pride. Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, hears about Jesus and decides that he must be “John the Baptist; he has been raised from the dead.” The Evangelist then tells why he thinks so. John had been arrested because he had said to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have her,” meaning Herodias, his brother Philip's wife. Herod “wanted to put him to death,” but he “feared the crowd, because they regarded him as a prophet.” St Mark adds that Herod “feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man,” and “liked to listen to him” (Mark 6:20), though he did not act on what he heard. At his birthday banquet Herodias' daughter dances, and Herod, carried away, promises with an oath to give her whatever she asks. Prompted by her mother she says: “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” The king is “grieved, yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests” he orders it. What a picture of a man who is a king and a slave: afraid of the crowd, afraid of the guests, afraid of looking weak, and not afraid of killing a righteous man. John, in prison, had the freedom Herod lacked. The scene ends with a detail of great tenderness: John's disciples “took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus.” They bring their grief to him. Today the Church remembers St Ignatius of Loyola, a man who knew the power of such a decision. Born in 1491 in the Basque country, a courtier and soldier, Ignatius was wounded by a cannonball at Pamplona in 1521. While he recovered at Loyola he read the lives of Christ and of the saints, and noticed that the thoughts of serving God left him peaceful and joyful, while worldly dreams left him empty. That was the beginning of his conversion and of his teaching on the discernment of spirits. At Manresa he began to write the Spiritual Exercises; he studied in Spain and Paris, and gathered friends, among them St Francis Xavier and St Peter Faber; and the Society of Jesus was approved by Pope Paul III in 1540. Ignatius died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622. His watchword was “for the greater glory of God,” in Latin Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, which is St Paul's line in the proper reading: “whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” The Jesuits have long served India: St Francis Xavier landed at Goa in 1542 and worked among the fishing communities of the coast, and Jesuit schools and colleges are found in every part of the country. The proper Gospel for the memorial is Jesus' call to count the cost: “Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.” Ignatius knew that real freedom is the freedom to give oneself wholly to God.
outline: Ask: where in your life do you need to hear the trumpet of the Jubilee: to be released, or to release someone?
Return to your property and family; no cheating; the Lord's favour proclaimed to the poor.

St Ignatius: wounded at Pamplona, converted at Loyola, and given wholly to God.
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.”
live: Forgive a debt, a wrong or a grievance this week, or release someone from an expectation you have placed on them.
Do it for God's glory (1 Corinthians 10:31)
Before each task today, say: for the greater glory of God. Do one ordinary task carefully for that sake alone.
saints: Basque soldier, wounded at Pamplona in 1521, converted at Loyola, author of the Spiritual Exercises, founder of the Society of Jesus (approved 1540) and its first Superior General. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised on 12 March 1622. His motto: for the greater glory of God. Patron of retreats and of soldiers.
2027-07-31.prayer: O God, who raised up Saint Ignatius of Loyola in your Church to further the greater glory of your name, grant that by his help we may imitate him in fighting the good fight on earth and merit to receive with him a crown in heaven. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray with Ignatius: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding and my entire will. Give me only your love and your grace, and I am rich enough. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the trumpet of the Jubilee sounds: “Lift up your hearts.” The Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world, and in Communion we are given liberty to return to our true home. St Ignatius used to say the Mass with great devotion and, in his Exercises, taught the prayer that sums up Christian freedom: Take, Lord, and receive. At the altar we make that prayer our own, giving back to God what he has given, and receiving him who gives himself. All things are offered for the greater glory of God.

quick: The law of the Jubilee: every fiftieth year the trumpet proclaims liberty and every family returns to its land.
Herod Antipas, afraid of the crowd and of his guests, has John the Baptist beheaded in prison.
St Ignatius of Loyola, converted by a wound, founds the Society of Jesus for the greater glory of God.
2027-07-31.action: Forgive a debt or a wrong today, as the Jubilee asks, and do one task for the glory of God.
2027-07-31.question: Whose freedom or good name am I keeping back, and what am I afraid to lose?
kidsaint: Ignatius was a soldier in Spain who dreamed of fame. One day a cannonball hurt his leg very badly, and he had to stay in bed for months. There was nothing to read except books about Jesus and the saints. He began to think: the saints did great things for God. I can too! So he gave his life to God, and he gathered friends who wanted to help others for God's glory. They were called Jesuits. One of them, Francis Xavier, went all the way to India. Ignatius had a saying: for the greater glory of God. Lesson: even a hurt, when given to God, can turn into a new beginning.

family.explain: King Herod had put John the Baptist in prison because John told him the truth. Herod was afraid of what people thought. At a big party he made a rash promise, and because he did not want to look foolish in front of his guests, he did something very wrong. John was a brave man who told the truth even though it cost him his life. His friends took care of his body and went and told Jesus. We can always bring our sadness to Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for people who suffer for telling the truth, and for those who are afraid to do what is right.
family.ask: Ask: “Have we ever been afraid to do the right thing because of what others would say? How can we be braver?”

illus: A schoolboy in a Jesuit school in Tamil Nadu used to write A.M.D.G. at the top of every exercise book. His teacher, an old Jesuit brother, told him that it stood for the greater glory of God. Years later the boy, now a doctor in a village clinic in Kerala, wrote the same letters on the first page of every patient's file. When a young nurse asked what they meant, he said: they remind me that the patient is not here for my glory, or for the clinic's, but because God wishes to be glorified in someone's recovery. The nurse began writing the letters too. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord of the Jubilee, release us from fear and from the need to please others, and teach us to do everything for your greater glory. Amen.
share: You shall proclaim liberty throughout the land (Leviticus 25:10). Whom do I need to release, or from what do I need to be released?
Herod feared the crowd and his guests (Matthew 14:5, 9). Where does the fear of what others think hold me back from doing right?
Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). What ordinary task will I do for God's glory today?
pm.resp: O God, let all the nations praise you!
interc: For the Church, that she may proclaim liberty to captives and good news to the poor.
For the Society of Jesus and all religious, that they may serve for the greater glory of God.
For those who are imprisoned unjustly, and for those who suffer for speaking the truth.
For those who are bound by debt, fear or addiction, that they may know the freedom of the children of God.
For our group, that we may do everything for the glory of God.
pm.close: God and Father of all nations, you sent your Son to proclaim liberty. By the prayers of St Ignatius, give us liberty to offer ourselves wholly to you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, God gives Israel a wonderful law in the book of Leviticus: the Jubilee. Every fiftieth year the trumpet is sounded across the land, and everyone is to return to their property and to their family (Leviticus 25:10). Debts are cancelled, slaves are released, the land rests. It is a year of liberty. Jesus would read from Isaiah in Nazareth about this very year: to proclaim release to the captives, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor (Luke 4:18–19). And the Church keeps Jubilee Holy Years to remind us that God's mercy is always opening doors.

The Gospel shows the opposite. Herod is a king, and he has no liberty. He is afraid of the crowd. He is afraid of his guests. He is afraid of his oath, and so he orders the death of a righteous man. And in prison there is John, who has nothing but the truth, and he is the one at liberty. It is not lawful for you to have her (Matthew 14:4). John did not fear to say what was right, and he paid for it with his life. This is the freedom of the Jubilee: not to be spared the consequences, but to be released from fear.

At the end of the passage there is a small detail: his disciples took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus (Matthew 14:12). They bring their grief to Jesus. That is where every sorrow should go.

Today we remember a man who found this freedom: St Ignatius of Loyola. A proud soldier, he was wounded at Pamplona. In bed, with nothing to read but the lives of Christ and the saints, he found that thoughts of serving God left him with a deep peace. His whole life was changed. He wrote the Spiritual Exercises, and gathered friends like Francis Xavier, who came to India, to Goa, to the fishermen of our coasts. His motto was for the greater glory of God. St Paul says it: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Dear friends, let us ask for the Jubilee freedom of Ignatius and John: released from fear, ready to give ourselves wholly, for the greater glory of God. Amen.
kids: Children, Ignatius was a soldier who wanted to be famous. But a cannonball hurt his leg and he had to stay in bed for a long time. He read books about Jesus and the saints, and he decided to give his life to God instead. He started a group of friends who wanted to do everything for God's glory. They were called Jesuits, and one of them, Francis Xavier, travelled all the way to India. Ignatius used to say: for the greater glory of God. Today let us do something very small, like tidying our room, and say: for the glory of God!

intro: Theme: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.”
The year of Jubilee, a king enslaved by fear and a prophet at liberty in prison, and St Ignatius: liberty is to give oneself wholly to God.

points.h: For the greater glory of God
sub: The Society of Jesus and the road to India.
q: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness.
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
points.apply: Begin each day this week with a short offering: Lord, all for your greater glory.

concl: The Jubilee proclaims that God releases his people, restores what was lost and keeps every family at home in the land.
St Ignatius found freedom in giving himself wholly to God, and shows that whatever we do can be done for his glory.
2027-07-31.resolve: Begin each day with the offering: for the greater glory of God, and forgive one person who has wronged you.
